claims.head: The matchup inside the matchup
claims.body: The Oilers are the league’s best for the power play, but the Hurricanes are one of the best at the penalty kill. Our lean: the Oilers’ power play wins out. Power plays usually beat kills in these spots. Edmonton has had one of the league’s most effective power plays, and Carolina has had one of the league’s best penalty kills for years.

claims.body: The Hurricanes have been the league’s best at controlling the chances at 5-on-5, and the Oilers around the middle. Expect the Hurricanes to spend more of the night in the Oilers’ end. CAR.head: This one sets up well for the Hurricanes
CAR.body: Carolina has been out-chancing opponents by a wide margin lately and has home-ice advantage. The Oilers’ best way in is keeping dangerous shots away.

EDM.head: A steep climb for the Oilers
EDM.body: Carolina has been out-chancing opponents by a wide margin lately and has home-ice advantage. The Oilers can still win it if they keep dangerous shots away, but a lot has to go their way.

story.head: Two good teams
paras: The Oilers won the teams’ first meeting this season, 6-5 in a shootout in Edmonton on Oct 22. The Oilers (17-4-3) lost 3-1 to Tampa Bay on Thursday, and the Hurricanes (16-3-3) lost 2-1 in overtime to Montréal the same night. Two good teams meet. Going in, the Oilers are first in the Pacific (second in the NHL) and the Hurricanes first in the Metropolitan (third).
The Oilers’ record (.771) is running ahead of what their chances are worth (.560), largely thanks to their finishing. The Hurricanes’ record (.795) is about what their chances are worth.

The Oilers lean on their stars more than any team in the league (lowest) and play slow, tight games (3rd lowest). They also have the league’s most dangerous power play (1st), and their power play against the Hurricanes’ penalty killers is strength against strength. Edmonton has scored 3.83 goals a game, the third most in the league. On the other side, the Hurricanes take away shots from the point (lowest) and create more chances on the penalty kill than anyone (1st), but give up a lot of dangerous shots (32nd). Carolina has scored 4.00 goals a game, the most in the league, and allowed 2.18, the second fewest. That means the Canes roll four lines, but the Oilers lean on their top six.

Connor McDavid (13 G / 42 A / 55 P in 24 GP) leads the Oilers and the whole NHL in scoring, with seven points in his last five games and a point in seven straight games against Carolina. Leon Draisaitl (21 G / 23 A / 44 P in 24 GP) has a team-high 21 goals, tied for the most in the NHL, with eight points in his last five games. Sebastian Aho (12 G / 17 A / 29 P in 22 GP) leads the Hurricanes in scoring and is tied for tenth in the NHL, with eight points in his last five games. Andrei Svechnikov (11 G / 10 A / 21 P in 22 GP) isn’t far behind, with seven points in his last five games.
Tristan Jarry (6-1-3 / .909 SV% in 10 GS) is expected to go for Edmonton. Pyotr Kochetkov (12-1-1 / .920 SV% in 14 GS) has been outstanding for Carolina and is expected to start.

At home, Rod Brind'Amour likes to send Hall, Jankowski and Robinson out against opponents’ fourth lines, so watch for them against Formenton, Michaels and Joseph. Elsewhere, the Hurricanes usually control more of the chances than the Oilers do.
